text: In the early nineteen-fifties, thousands of people were turned away from Barcelona's stadium every other Sunday.
The ground at Les Corts had been expanded again and again, and it was still too small. Everyone wanted to see one man play.
So the club did something it could barely afford. It built the biggest stadium in Europe.
That stadium is the Camp Nou. And the man people came to see was a refugee who had escaped from behind the Iron Curtain hidden in the back of a truck.
This is the story of László Kubala — or, as Barcelona came to know him, Ladislao.
A player who represented three different national teams, was banned from football, starred in a film about his own life, and was later voted the greatest player in Barça's history.
Part one. Three countries.
Kubala was born in Budapest in nineteen twenty-seven, into a family with Slovak, Polish and Hungarian roots. That mixed background would shape his whole career.
He was a teenage star at Ferencváros, then moved to Slovan Bratislava, and played for Czechoslovakia.
Back in Budapest, he played for Hungary.
And later, after everything you're about to hear, he would play for Spain. Three national teams. It sounds impossible today. In post-war Europe, borders and passports were changing all the time.
He was strong, with heavy shoulders, but he was also astonishingly skilful. He could dribble through crowded spaces, strike the ball with either foot, and his free-kicks were famous for their curl.
People who saw him play describe a footballer who combined power and technique in a way that was rare for his time.
Part two. The escape.
By the late nineteen-forties, Hungary was becoming a communist state. Its borders were closing, and the best footballers were not allowed to leave.
Kubala decided to go anyway.
In January nineteen forty-nine, according to the story he later told, he escaped hidden in the back of a truck — some versions say wearing a Soviet army uniform — and crossed into Austria.
He made it to the American zone of occupation, and from there to Italy. He had a football career, a family, and no country.
From Budapest, through Austria, into Italy — and eventually, to Spain.
But first, there was a problem. The Hungarian football federation complained that he had left without permission and broken his contract. FIFA agreed, and banned him from playing official matches.
Part three. The refugee team.
Unable to play officially, Kubala did something remarkable. With other players who had fled Eastern Europe, he formed a team of exiles. They called it Hungaria.
They couldn't play in any league, so they played friendlies, travelling from town to town and earning whatever they could.
In nineteen fifty, the tour took them to Spain. They played in Madrid, against a Spanish national selection, and against Real Madrid. Kubala was the best player on the pitch.
Real Madrid tried to sign him. But Barcelona's technical secretary, the former star Josep Samitier, moved faster.
In June nineteen fifty, Kubala signed for FC Barcelona. Because of the ban, he still couldn't play official games right away.
It took time and negotiation to clear it. He was given Spanish nationality, the ban was lifted, and in nineteen fifty-one, he finally made his official debut.
Part four. The five cups.
It didn't take long for him to show what he could do. In February nineteen fifty-two, against Sporting Gijón, he scored seven goals in a single league match.
More than seventy years later, it's still the record for the most goals by one player in a La Liga game. Not Messi, not Ronaldo, not anyone has beaten it.
That season, Barcelona won the league, the Spanish Cup, and the Latin Cup — a tournament between the champions of Spain, France, Italy and Portugal, one of the forerunners of the European Cup.
They also won two smaller trophies. Five cups in one season. In Barcelona, that team is still remembered by a single name: the Barça of the Five Cups.
And at the centre of it was Kubala — scoring, creating, taking the free-kicks that made crowds hold their breath.
Part five. The stadium.
Les Corts had been Barcelona's home since the nineteen-twenties. Every time it was expanded, it filled up again.
With Kubala playing, demand for tickets was far greater than the stadium could hold. The club's members began to push for something new — something huge.
Construction started in nineteen fifty-four. And on the twenty-fourth of September, nineteen fifty-seven, the Camp Nou opened — the largest stadium in Europe.
In Barcelona, there's a saying that every supporter knows: Kubala built the Camp Nou.
He didn't lay a single brick, of course. But without the crowds he drew, the club would not have dared to build it, and the members would not have paid for it.
Almost seventy years later, when the Camp Nou was rebuilt, it was still the stadium that Kubala's fans made necessary.
Part six. The film star.
By the mid-fifties, Kubala was so famous in Spain that a film was made about his life — and he played himself.
It was called Los ases buscan la paz — The Stars Search for Peace — and it told the story of his escape from Hungary.
It's a strange thing to think about today. A footballer starring in a movie about his own escape, while he was still playing. But it tells you how big his story had become.
He also played for Spain, scoring in his international appearances in the fifties, although Spain failed to qualify for the World Cups of his era.
It was one of the few things missing from a career that had already given him almost everything else.
Part seven. Di Stéfano.
In nineteen fifty-three, Barcelona tried to sign another great player — Alfredo Di Stéfano.
What happened next is one of the most controversial stories in football history. Di Stéfano ended up at Real Madrid, and helped them win five European Cups in a row.
It's a story so complicated that it needs its own episode — and it will get one on this channel.
But it changed the balance of Spanish football, and it turned the rivalry between Barcelona and Madrid into something much bigger than football.
Part eight. Legacy.
Kubala's later years at Barça were complicated, with arguments with coaches and a slow, painful decline. He left the club as a player at the start of the nineteen-sixties.
He went on to coach, and from nineteen sixty-nine he led Spain's national team for more than a decade — one of the longest spells of any Spain coach.

In nineteen ninety-nine, for the club's hundredth anniversary, Barça supporters were asked to vote for the greatest player in the club's history. They chose Kubala — ahead of Cruyff, ahead of Maradona.
He died in Barcelona in May two thousand and two. Today, a statue of him stands outside the Camp Nou, frozen in the moment of striking a ball.
Think about it. A man who arrived in Spain with no country, banned from playing, travelling with a team of exiles.
And he left behind a stadium for a hundred thousand people, a record that has lasted for more than seventy years, and a club that had become one of the biggest in the world.
Before Cruyff, before Messi, there was Kubala. And without him, the stage they played on might never have been built.
The fans of nineteen ninety-nine chose Kubala. Who's your greatest ever? Tell me in the comments.
And for the man who came next — and changed everything again — watch The Full Story of Johan Cruyff.
